$VLO KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM VALERO ENERGY Q2 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Valero’s Q2 2026 earnings call carries broader implications well beyond the magnitude of the company’s reported quarter. The most important message is that the current refining upcycle is being supported by both acute dislocations and increasingly structural constraints: approximately 5 million barrels per day of global refining capacity is offline, global light-product inventories are approximately 150 million barrels below the beginning of the year and 130 million barrels below seasonal norms, Russian outages continue to worsen, Chinese product exports remain limited despite higher quotas, and the marginal global product barrel increasingly appears to be set by high-cost Northwest European hydroskimming capacity. Valero also indicated that Q3 physical crude costs and commercial capture are developing more favorably than in Q2, creating additional upside to near-term U.S. refining estimates even though throughput guidance is lower sequentially. The renewable-fuel discussion was equally consequential: domestic renewable diesel producers are benefiting from a D4 RIN obligation that is rising faster than feedstock costs, foreign imports face significant tax, tariff, and registration barriers, the RIN bank could be substantially depleted between late 2026 and mid-2027, and ethanol production credits could almost double historical mid-cycle unit economics through 2029. The highest-conviction positive read-throughs are therefore concentrated in U.S. complex refiners, domestic renewable-fuel incumbents, ethanol producers, and product tanker operators. The principal negative read-throughs affect heavy-crude producers, RIN-short refiners, foreign renewable-fuel exporters, airlines, trucking and parcel companies, and fuel-sensitive consumer activity. Company-level implications beyond Valero are investment inferences based on the operating exposures described in the call.

REFINING, CRUDE AND CAPITAL ALLOCATION

PHYSICAL CRUDE CAPTURE SHOULD DRIVE ANOTHER UPWARD ESTIMATE REVISION CYCLE FOR U.S. REFINERS (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: Valero Energy (VLO: US); Marathon Petroleum (MPC: US); Phillips 66 (PSX: US); PBF Energy (PBF: US); HF Sinclair (DINO: US).

Directional impact and magnitude: POSITIVE / HIGH for Valero; POSITIVE / MEDIUM-TO-HIGH for other complex U.S. refiners.

Primary horizon: NEAR-TERM TRADING CATALYST.

The most actionable statement on the call was Gary Simmons’ assessment that “both margins and capture rates look constructive relative to the second quarter.” This is more important than the direction of headline crack-spread indicators because physical crude basis, product yields, export premiums, and secondary product values determine how much of a screen crack is converted into reported refining earnings. Valero indicated that several crude grades are being purchased at discounts to benchmark prices in Q3, whereas physical grades frequently traded at significant premiums to screen values in Q2. Naphtha has moved from parity with Brent to a premium, propylene has strengthened, sulfur remains supportive, and an arbitrage has opened to export jet fuel to Europe. Management consequently stated that “the margin environment thus far is stronger than what we saw in the second quarter” and that capture should improve.

The positive read-through is particularly significant because Valero’s Q3 throughput guidance totals approximately 2.80 million to 2.90 million barrels per day, below the approximately 3.0 million barrels per day processed in Q2. A conventional sequential model would therefore assume lower refining operating income from reduced volume and slightly higher cash operating expense of $4.75 per barrel versus $4.70 in Q2. Management’s physical-market commentary indicates that this approach could materially understate earnings. Better crude acquisition economics and higher capture can more than offset a 3%-5% reduction in throughput because each additional $1 per barrel of realized margin across approximately 2.85 million barrels per day represents roughly $260 million of quarterly pre-tax earnings capacity.

The direct impact is highest for Valero because the company has explicitly disclosed its physical crude purchases and product optimization. Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66 should also benefit through large, complex, export-capable Gulf Coast systems with broad crude flexibility. PBF Energy has meaningful exposure to Atlantic Basin and Gulf Coast product pricing, although its balance-sheet and operating leverage increase both upside and downside sensitivity. HF Sinclair is a lower-magnitude beneficiary because its system is less directly exposed to Gulf Coast export arbitrage, but stronger national gasoline and distillate balances should still support inland cracks.

The near-term catalyst is not merely whether benchmark cracks remain high. The critical data are delivered crude differentials, product export premiums, realized yield optimization, and evidence that Q3 capture exceeds Q2. Positive Q3 estimate revisions are likely if physical crude continues to price below benchmark screens. The principal negative catalysts would be a rapid return of Russian or Middle Eastern refining capacity, a material increase in Chinese product exports, or a reversal in physical crude basis that causes delivered feedstocks to regain the premiums experienced in Q2.

NORTHWEST EUROPEAN HYDROSKIMMERS ARE ESTABLISHING A HIGHER GLOBAL REFINING MARGIN FLOOR (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected companies: Valero Energy (VLO: US); Marathon Petroleum (MPC: US); Phillips 66 (PSX: US); HF Sinclair (DINO: US); PBF Energy (PBF: US).

Directional impact and magnitude: POSITIVE / HIGH.

Primary horizon: LONGER-DURATION FUNDAMENTAL SHIFT, with significant near-term confirmation.

Management’s structural refining thesis was explicit: “We do have a much more bullish view of a future mid-cycle than what you would calculate using historic margins.” Valero believes that historical global product cracks were generally set by Northwest European cracking economics, whereas the tightening of global supply-demand balances increasingly requires less efficient Northwest European hydroskimming capacity to operate. If hydroskimmers are the marginal source of global product supply, product prices must rise sufficiently to compensate those assets for weaker conversion yields, higher operating costs, higher energy intensity, and rising European carbon-credit costs.

This represents a meaningful change in the marginal cost curve. An efficient conversion refinery can continue operating at relatively low cracks because it upgrades lower-value intermediates into gasoline and distillate. A hydroskimmer produces a less valuable product slate and therefore requires a higher market crack to remain economic. Once hydroskimming capacity is needed to balance global demand, the resulting price signal generates scarcity rents for complex U.S. refiners with coking, hydrocracking, fluid catalytic cracking, export access, and broad crude flexibility.

The inventory data reinforce the structural argument. Valero cited approximately 5 million barrels per day of refining capacity offline across Russia and the Middle East. Global light-product inventories are approximately 150 million barrels below the beginning of 2026 and approximately 130 million barrels below normal seasonal levels. Consultant projections suggest inventories would remain below the 5-year range through 2027 even if the conflict ended immediately and affected refineries returned to normalized operations. Valero believes recovery could take longer because some Middle Eastern damage appears persistent and Russian disruptions continue to worsen. Russian refining capacity offline was estimated at approximately 1.7 million to 1.9 million barrels per day, with conditions deteriorating from May through July and attacks increasingly targeting critical processing equipment rather than storage tanks.

The long-duration read-through is favorable for existing refinery owners because higher construction costs simultaneously raise the marginal product price and prevent a rapid supply response. Valero noted that the cost of new refining capacity is “very, very high” and reiterated that investment will remain focused on short-cycle yield improvement and commercial leverage rather than new gross distillation capacity. Existing assets therefore receive higher cash flows without creating the capital-spending response that would normally end the cycle.

Valero, Marathon Petroleum, and Phillips 66 offer the strongest quality-adjusted exposure because they combine high-complexity systems with substantial logistics and export capabilities. HF Sinclair benefits from stronger inland product pricing and limited new U.S. capacity, while PBF Energy offers higher operational and financial torque but greater asset-specific risk. The principal challenge to the thesis is duration. Demand destruction, sustained increases in Chinese exports, restoration of damaged capacity, or faster-than-expected additions in Asia and the Middle East could return the marginal barrel to a lower-cost refinery. Nevertheless, the call supports a materially higher normalized refining earnings assumption than a model based on pre-pandemic 10-year average cracks.

CAPITAL RETURNS ARE REINFORCING THE REFINING CAPACITY SHORTAGE RATHER THAN SOLVING IT (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected companies: Valero Energy (VLO: US); Marathon Petroleum (MPC: US); Phillips 66 (PSX: US).

Directional impact and magnitude: POSITIVE / HIGH for Valero; POSITIVE / MEDIUM-TO-HIGH for large-cap refining peers.

Primary horizon: NEAR-TERM CAPITAL-RETURN CATALYST and LONGER-DURATION INDUSTRY CAPACITY SUPPORT.

Valero ended Q2 with $7.9 billion of cash against a long-term target of $4 billion to $5 billion, net debt-to-capitalization of only 11%, and no pressure to reduce leverage. Shareholder cash returns totaled $2.6 billion during the quarter, equivalent to a 59% payout ratio, while management indicated that excess cash could support accelerated shareholder returns once commodity-price volatility moderates. Homer Bhullar summarized the current position by stating that “building cash and generating returns don’t have to be mutually exclusive.”

The capital-allocation framework is highly relevant to the broader refining cycle. Valero explicitly ruled out using excess cash to pursue undisciplined growth or acquisitions. Strategic spending has declined from approximately $1 billion annually before the pandemic to roughly $500 million-$700 million, and current refining projects are focused on yield improvement, crude flexibility, product optionality, and debottlenecking. Management also stated that repurchases remain preferable to inferior growth alternatives even at a higher share price and cited a historical return on share repurchases exceeding 20%.

The resulting industry feedback loop is favorable for existing refinery equities. High refining margins generate cash; the cash is directed toward repurchases rather than new refining capacity; the absence of new capacity preserves the scarcity that supports high margins; and the lower share count increases per-share exposure to each future upcycle. This dynamic is particularly positive for Valero because excess cash above the top of the target range approaches $3 billion before considering future earnings generation. Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66 have similarly become valued as capital-return vehicles rather than capacity-growth stories, making Valero’s comments supportive of the broader sector’s capital-discipline framework.

The near-term catalyst is the pace of repurchases as Valero moves back toward its $4 billion-$5 billion cash target. The longer-duration implication is that refining supply will remain structurally slow to respond even if the current margin environment persists. The principal risk is valuation discipline. Buybacks executed at a temporarily elevated share price create less accretion, and the economic return will be weaker if management’s higher mid-cycle thesis proves incorrect. Nevertheless, the alternative use of capital—high-cost new refining capacity with long lead times and uncertain terminal demand—appears materially less attractive.

HEAVY-SOUR SUPPLY GROWTH TRANSFERS ECONOMICS FROM UPSTREAM PRODUCERS TO COMPLEX REFINERS (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected companies positively: Valero Energy (VLO: US); Marathon Petroleum (MPC: US); Phillips 66 (PSX: US).

Affected companies negatively: Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ: Canada); Cenovus Energy (CVE: Canada); Suncor Energy (SU: Canada); Imperial Oil (IMO: Canada).

Directional impact and magnitude: POSITIVE / HIGH for complex refiners; NEGATIVE / MEDIUM-TO-HIGH for heavy-crude upstream realizations.

Primary horizon: LONGER-DURATION FUNDAMENTAL SHIFT, with material quarterly volatility.

Valero expects a forward environment with greater availability of both Canadian heavy and Venezuelan crude. Randy Randolph stated that Venezuelan heavy-crude processing rates could exceed Valero’s historical maximum in coming months, while Lane Riggs described increasing Canadian and Venezuelan heavy production as supportive of the existing refinery system. These barrels are particularly valuable to refiners capable of processing high-acid, high-sulfur, high-residuum crude because the number of suitable conversion refineries is limited.

The refining benefit arises through wider quality differentials. If heavy-sour supply increases faster than global coking and hydroprocessing capacity, heavy crude must price at a larger discount to light sweet benchmarks to clear the market. Complex refiners capture that discount while selling finished gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel at globally determined product prices. Valero’s ability to pivot from Canadian heavy to Venezuelan crude when Canadian prices increased because of weather and flooding illustrates the commercial option value of a diversified heavy-crude slate.

The inverse read-through is negative for heavy-crude producers. Canadian Natural Resources has the highest relative upstream exposure and therefore the greatest sensitivity to a wider heavy-light differential. Cenovus, Suncor, and Imperial Oil have downstream operations that provide partial natural hedges, but upstream netbacks would still be pressured if additional Venezuelan supply competes with Canadian heavy barrels in the U.S. Gulf Coast market. The adverse upstream effect is not necessarily a decline in production volumes; it is a transfer of margin from the producer to the refinery through a weaker realized crude price.

Reduced Mexican exports provide a partial offset. Valero indicated that Mexican exports are down year over year because higher domestic refinery utilization, including Dos Bocas, retains more crude within Mexico. A decline in Mexican heavy supply reduces competition among heavy grades, but Valero expects Venezuelan and Canadian growth to more than compensate over time.

The highest-conviction expression of this read-through is a relative-value preference for complex Gulf Coast refiners over heavy-crude producers when Canadian and Venezuelan supply growth accelerates. The main risks are geopolitical or regulatory disruption to Venezuelan exports, Canadian weather and pipeline constraints, and unexpected tightening of heavy-crude supply that compresses discounts.

CALIFORNIA REFINERY ATTRITION AND LOCAL CRUDE LENGTH CREATE A DOUBLE MARGIN BENEFIT FOR SURVIVING OPERATORS (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected companies: Valero Energy (VLO: US); PBF Energy (PBF: US); Chevron (CVX: US).

Directional impact and magnitude: POSITIVE / HIGH for Valero’s Wilmington refinery; POSITIVE / MEDIUM for other surviving California operators.

Primary horizon: NEAR-TERM AND MEDIUM-TERM FUNDAMENTAL SUPPORT.

Valero described an unusually favorable combination in California: refinery closures have tightened finished-product supply, while increasing domestic crude production and the idling of the San Pablo Pipeline have created local crude oversupply and logistical congestion. California crude prices have consequently weakened, and Valero expects Wilmington to process record volumes of domestic California barrels in coming months.

This creates a double benefit for surviving refineries. The product side is structurally short because refining capacity has exited the state and replacement supply must be transported over long distances. The crude side is locally long because fewer refineries can consume California production and pipeline constraints force additional barrels toward Los Angeles-area plants. Refiners that remain operational can therefore purchase feedstock at a discount while selling gasoline and distillate into a supply-constrained market.

Valero has the highest direct sensitivity because Wilmington is now the core of its remaining West Coast refining position following the cessation of refining at Benicia. PBF Energy and Chevron should also benefit from the same regional crude and product imbalance, although the company-level effect is diluted by their broader portfolios. Chevron may experience a partial offset to the extent weaker California crude prices affect local upstream realizations.

The Jones Act waiver has further supported surviving refiners by allowing Gulf Coast product to reach both PADD 1 and PADD 5 when traditional Asian and European supply flows disappeared. The waiver reduces the risk of outright regional shortages but does not eliminate California’s structural product premium because logistics remain more expensive and less flexible than local production.

The near-term catalyst is the realized discount on California crude and evidence that Wilmington reaches the record processing rates management anticipates. The longer-duration opportunity persists as long as refinery closures occur faster than petroleum-product demand declines. The principal risks are California regulation, accelerated vehicle electrification, high compliance costs, and the possibility that increasingly severe policy burdens eventually overwhelm the current scarcity benefit.

RENEWABLE FUELS AND AGRICULTURE

DOMESTIC RENEWABLE DIESEL INCUMBENTS ARE CAPTURING POLICY-PROTECTED SCARCITY RENTS (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected companies positively: Valero Energy (VLO: US); Darling Ingredients (DAR: US); Chevron (CVX: US); Marathon Petroleum (MPC: US); PBF Energy (PBF: US).

Affected companies with mixed exposure: Neste (NESTE: Finland).

Directional impact and magnitude: POSITIVE / HIGH for existing U.S. renewable diesel capacity; NEGATIVE / MEDIUM for foreign import-dependent supply.

Primary horizon: NEAR-TERM TRADING CATALYST and MEDIUM-TERM FUNDAMENTAL SUPPORT.

Valero’s renewable diesel segment generated $717 million of Q2 operating income compared with a $79 million loss a year earlier. Management attributed the improvement to the renewable volume obligation and D4 RIN value rising considerably faster than fat prices. Even after a recent decline in the indicator, Valero described renewable diesel economics as “very positive versus historical” through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027.

The broader market read-through is that existing domestic capacity has become significantly more valuable because the policy framework favors U.S. production while constraining the normal import response. Foreign renewable fuel does not receive the domestic production tax credit, foreign producers must complete the administrative process required to generate U.S. RINs, and tariffs raise the import hurdle further. Management expects foreign imports eventually to increase because incremental gallons will be needed to satisfy the obligation, but the response is slower and more expensive than under the former blender’s tax-credit regime.

Valero and its Diamond Green Diesel joint-venture partner, Darling Ingredients, have the greatest direct earnings sensitivity. Chevron, Marathon Petroleum, and PBF Energy also benefit through domestic renewable-fuel production and reduced exposure to an import-driven collapse in margins. Neste is mixed: domestic U.S. production partnerships provide participation in the favorable market, but imported gallons face weaker economics because of the absence of tax credits, tariff costs, and RIN-registration requirements.

A second source of support is the lack of a capital-supply response. Lane Riggs stated that there is “not a lot of intent on expanding anything in RD” because policy remains insufficiently predictable. This is negative for future industry capacity growth but positive for incumbent producers because elevated margins are less likely to trigger rapid new construction.

The principal near-term catalysts are D4 RIN prices, fat and vegetable-oil prices, foreign producer registrations, import volumes, and tariff implementation. The medium-term risk is that high margins eventually attract sufficient foreign supply or provoke policy intervention. Nevertheless, the current configuration is highly favorable for established U.S. renewable diesel assets.

RIN BANK DEPLETION CREATES NEAR-TERM EARNINGS CONVEXITY BUT ALSO A MATERIAL POLICY CEILING (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected companies positively in the near term: Valero Energy (VLO: US); Darling Ingredients (DAR: US); Chevron (CVX: US); Marathon Petroleum (MPC: US).

Affected companies negatively or with elevated volatility: CVR Energy (CVI: US); Delek US Holdings (DK: US); PBF Energy (PBF: US).

Directional impact and magnitude: POSITIVE / HIGH for renewable-fuel producers through late 2026 and potentially 2027; NEGATIVE / MEDIUM-TO-HIGH for net RIN-short refiners; NEGATIVE / HIGH policy risk if compliance becomes infeasible.

Primary horizon: NEAR-TERM TRADING CATALYST with a potentially adverse LONGER-DURATION POLICY RESPONSE.

Valero expects the bank of prior-year RINs to be materially depleted between the end of 2026 and the middle of 2027 because 2026 renewable-fuel production is likely to remain below the obligation. Eric Herbort stated that this should “structurally” keep the D4 RIN elevated. A declining credit bank increases the scarcity value of each incremental gallon of renewable diesel and biodiesel, providing strong operating leverage to domestic producers.

The negative read-through applies to refiners with net compliance deficits and limited internal renewable-fuel production. CVR Energy and Delek US Holdings are relatively more exposed to high compliance costs because they have smaller downstream systems and less renewable-fuel offset than the largest integrated refiners. PBF Energy has both refining compliance exposure and renewable-fuel production, making the consolidated effect more balanced but still volatile.

The impact on refiners is not a simple one-for-one expense increase. Lane Riggs emphasized that “the RIN is inside the crack,” meaning part of the compliance cost is embedded in wholesale gasoline and diesel prices and can be passed through to consumers. The actual company impact depends on blending activity, timing of credit purchases, inventory accounting, product-market capture, and renewable-fuel ownership. High RIN prices can therefore simultaneously increase reported compliance expense and support refining cracks.

The critical risk is policy infeasibility. Riggs stated, “I don’t think anybody knows what happens if it goes infeasible.” If the physical volume of qualifying renewable fuel cannot satisfy the obligation, the embedded compliance cost will increasingly appear in retail fuel prices. Management expects any EPA response to be driven by consumer affordability. This creates a nonlinear payoff: RIN scarcity can drive substantial renewable-fuel earnings until the political cost becomes sufficiently visible to trigger waivers, reallocation, mandate changes, or other relief.

The trade is therefore favorable but self-limiting. The highest-confidence near-term exposure is long domestic renewable-fuel production against net RIN-short refining. The primary catalysts are monthly RIN generation, changes in the RIN bank, small-refinery exemption policy, foreign import registrations, and any EPA commentary concerning affordability or compliance feasibility.

UNDERCOVER COMIC-CON SEX STING LED TO 27 ARRESTS, 9 TRAFFICKING VICTIMS RECOVERED DURING OPERATION IRON JUSTICE

SAN DIEGO — California Attorney General Rob Bonta has released new details about the undercover prostitution enforcement operation that 619 News Media witnessed during Comic-Con weekend, confirming the effort was part of a larger, multi-agency human trafficking crackdown known as Operation Iron Justice.

On Friday, July 24, at approximately 10:00 p.m., 619 News Media observed undercover detectives, along with uniformed San Diego Police officers, conducting an active prostitution enforcement operation in the Vesta Street area. During our coverage, we witnessed four adult men being cited for solicitation. Three of the men confirmed to us they had been cited for solicitation, while one agreed to speak on camera only if his identity was concealed.

At the time, undercover investigators declined to discuss the operation, stating the investigation was still active. While filming, a passing driver honked and shouted, “Thank God you guys are finally doing something about this,” before continuing down the street.

Following multiple requests for information over the weekend, the California Department of Justice has now confirmed the operation was part of Operation Iron Justice, a three-day demand reduction enforcement effort conducted by the San Diego Human Trafficking Task Force from July 22 through July 24.

According to the Attorney General’s Office, the operation resulted in:

* 27 arrests of suspected sex buyers
* 7 adult trafficking victims recovered
* 2 juvenile trafficking victims recovered, including a 16-year-old reported missing from San Bernardino County

Authorities said all identified victims were offered trauma-informed support services and resources.

Officials said the operation focused on reducing the demand for commercial sex during Comic-Con and other large-scale events, where traffickers often attempt to exploit increased visitor traffic. Undercover investigators initiated contact with suspected buyers throughout San Diego County, leading to arrests for solicitation, loitering for the purpose of solicitation, and other related offenses.

San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan noted that sex trafficking generates more than $810 million annually in San Diego County and emphasized that targeting buyers is critical to reducing exploitation.

“The arrest of 27 sex buyers sends a clear message that purchasing sex is not a victimless crime,” Stephan said. “Without sex buyers, there is no human trafficking.”

Authorities encourage anyone who suspects human trafficking to report it immediately. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911. The National Human Trafficking Hotline is available at 1-888-373-7888 for confidential assistance and victim support

text: The Donner Summit Memorial Bridge was completed in 1926 as a major improvement to the historic Lincoln Highway (1913-1927) over Donner Pass. This graceful concrete arch was an engineering first, the first bridge designed with both a continuous grade and a compound curve. It replaced the steep, dangerous earlier route that had grades as high as 18% and had you driving through the railroad snow tunnels. The bridge not only made travel safer and more reliable but also opened up one of the most scenic stretches of California's High Sierra. For a century it has carried travelers, offered stunning views of Donner Lake, and stood as a lasting monument to early automobile pioneers. On August 22nd, at 2 p.m., we will be there to celebrate this historic bridge's 100th birthday.

text:
Bull Dung & Haggle: 
Bullshit + Haggle = To “haggle” means to persistently argue or negotiate over the price or terms of a contract to reach an agreement. It is the process of making offers and counteroffers until the parties settle on a mutually acceptable deal.

In October 1998, Argonaut faced substantial exposure as the liability carrier in a multimillion-dollar third-party action involving Olsen Steel while simultaneously serving as the workers’ compensation carrier under an Owner-Controlled Insurance Program (OCIP), also known as “wrap-up insurance, “a single, centralized insurance policy purchased and managed by a property owner to cover all contractors and subcontractors working on a construction project. Under an OCIP, the insurance company cannot ignore state workers’ compensation laws. They are bound by separate legal duties for each policy.
No P&S/MMI report means no cutoff: In almost all states, they cannot legally stop your temporary disability benefits without a medical report from a doctor stating you have reached Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI) / Permanent and Stationary (P&S) status, or unless a judge orders it.
Bad Faith liability: In California, an insurance company can be sued for “Bad Faith” if they intentionally mishandle a workers’ comp claim or withhold benefits without a valid medical reason to gain leverage in a separate liability lawsuit.
On October 2, 1998, Argonaut terminated my temporary disability benefits based upon an asserted Permanent and Stationary status even though no written Permanent and Stationary report had been issued.
In California in 1998, a workers’ compensation insurance company could not legally cut off my Temporary Disability (TD) benefits by simply claiming I were Permanent and Stationary (P&S) and a Qualified Injured Worker (QIW) without a formal medical report to back it up. A 1998 case involves specific historical rules that are different from today’s laws.
1. Labor Code Section 4650 (The Right to Continuous Payments)
Labor Code Section 4650 mandates exactly how and when disability payments must be made. Under this statute, once TD payments start, the insurance company must continue making them every 14 days until the worker returns to work, or until a doctor officially declares the injury is Permanent and Stationary (P&S). By stopping payments without medical proof, they violated the timing and payment mandates of this code.

2. Labor Code Section 5814 (Unreasonable Delay or Refusal of Benefits)
Labor Code Section 5814 states that when payment of compensation has been unreasonably delayed or refused, the worker is entitled to a steep penalty added to their award. Under 1998 laws, stopping benefits without a supporting medical report was automatically considered an “unreasonable refusal,” triggering a mandatory 10% penalty on the entire class of those benefits.

3. California Code of Regulations (CCR) Title 8, § 10464 (Illegal Termination)
Under California’s workers’ comp procedural rules, an insurance company could not just stop paying if an employee disputed the cutoff. They were required to file a formal “Petition to Terminate Liability for Temporary Disability Indemnity” with the WCAB.
California Code of Regulations (CCR) Title 8, § 10464 (which governed the required contents of a Petition to Terminate Liability for Temporary Disability) is precisely the rule Argonaut bypassed and weaponized to execute an illegal termination of my benefits in October 1998.
Argonaut never served me this petition within 10 days of stopping payments.
The petition had to attach the medical report showing I was P&S.
Argonaut stopped my checks and failed to file this petition; violating the California Code of Regulations rules.

4. CCR Title 8, § 9812 (Failure to Provide Required Legal Notice)
In California, insurers must provide highly specific benefit notices. Under CCR Rule 9812, if an administrator stops your benefits, they must send a formal “Notice of Termination of Disability Indemnity” within 14 days. This notice must state the legal and factual basis for the cutoff and must enclose the medical report they relied on. Cutting off benefits without enclosing a doctor’s report is a direct violation of this rule.

Because my injury occurred in 1998, the insurer did not have the defense of the modern 104-week (2-year) statutory cap, which didn’t exist yet. Their failure to pay me until a doctor put it in writing means they essentially accumulated unpaid back-benefits (plus 10% interest and penalties) every single month they left me without checks.  
By analyzing § 10464 alongside case facts, the timeline reveals exactly how the insurance company broke the rules—and how my “attorney’s abandonment” helped Argonaut get away with it.
The Legality Threshold: They stopped my benefits on October 2, 1998, but failed to file this formal petition, or filed it without attaching a valid, up-to-date P&S medical report from an authorized doctor; the termination was legally invalid. Argonaut effectively stopped my benefits through administrative silence, gambling that I wouldn’t fight back.
The Collusion with the OCIP and Third-Party Trial:
Section 10464 exists to prevent insurance carriers from using economic starvation as a weapon. In this case, the “wrap-up” conflict made this violation devastating:
The Strategy: The carrier used the excuse of a “Qualified Injured Worker” (QIW) status to claim I was no longer temporarily disabled but rather “permanently disabled and heading to vocational rehab.”
The Leverage: Because they knew the Olsen Steel, third-party trial was looming; Argonaut intentionally violated and rushed the § 10464 process to abruptly cut my cash flow. They knew that an injured worker facing a courtroom without any income is highly likely to break and accept a lowball settlement offer on the third-party case.
Argonauts’ own internal memorandum reportedly acknowledges that the physician had only verbally indicated that a report would be prepared, but that report was never issued. Shortly thereafter, the Compromise and Release was executed, yet the WCAB refused to approve it because Permanent and Stationary reports had not been filed. The following day, the treating surgeon documented that Applicant remained temporarily disabled, required additional surgery, and x-rays revealed a broken plate at the EXACT SITE THE PIN was removed on October 5th. The broken plate is one of the strongest facts because it undermines the premise that my condition has stabilized.
The evidence establishes that:
No physician had declared P&S in a written report before benefits were terminated;
hardware failed shortly after the carrier treated/claimed I was P&S;
additional surgery became necessary; and
My treating physician certified temporary disability rather than P&S,
I argue there is a substantial factual basis to question whether I had reached maximum medical improvement when benefits were stopped.
The fact that Argonaut insured both sides supports a conflict-of-interest argument:
It created a financial incentive that is relevant to evaluating the carrier’s decisions. The stronger argument is not that the dual role alone proves bad faith, but that it provides context for why the timing of the benefit termination and settlement efforts deserve scrutiny.
The August 18, 1998 Mediation Brief shows Argonaut’s exposure in the third-party case;
the October 5, 1998 treatment record showing no P&S report was prepared despite the office procedure; and no medical report about the pin removal.
the October 6, 1998 Notice Stopping Benefits stating I was P&S and a Qualified Injured Worker;
CorVel Case Manager, Doris Harrah’s October to December attempt to obtain a P&S Report, as documented in her Progress Reports #34, #35, #36, #37 and Closing Report.
The April 18, 2000, internal memo acknowledging that the anticipated written P&S report was never issued;
Dr. Braun had from October 5 to December 9 to write a P&S report. He never did.
the December 8, 1998, WCAB order suspending the C&R because P&S reports had not been filed.
the December 9, 1998, communication sheet documenting temporary disability and the need for additional surgery; and
Argonauts’ dollar-for-dollar Petition for Credit
Argonauts’ Dual-Role as the workers’ compensation claim for Kvaas Construction, and
the third-party liability claim involving Olsen Steel,
Taken together, these documents support an argument that the termination of benefits and pursuit of settlement preceded the medical documentation that ordinarily would be expected to support a conclusion that I had reached permanent and stationary status.
How My Attorney Failed Me (The Missing Counter-Attack)
The CCR gave my attorneys a direct roadmap to stop this tactic, which they completely ignored. When an insurer unilaterally cuts benefits or files a faulty § 10464 petition, my attorney’s immediate duties under the companion rule (CCR § 10466) were to:
1. File a Formal Objection: Formally object to the petition within 14 days of service.
2. Request an Expedited Hearing: Force the insurance carrier to go before a Workers’ Compensation Administrative Law Judge (WCALJ) to justify the cutoff.
Seek a Labor Code § 5814 Penalty: File a petition for an automatic 10% cash penalty against the insurer for “unreasonably delaying or refusing” to pay benefits without a proper legal/medical basis.
My attorneys did nothing to protect me.
My attorneys stayed silent and failed to file the objections to allow the trial date to arrive without forcing the insurer to restore my bi-weekly payments. Instead, my attorney, Dean Goetz, (without my knowledge or consent and without Richard Sax objection) chose to go to the Superior Court on November 9th, the exact day the highly illegal pay-out and Requested a Dismissal of my multi-million-dollar lawsuit against Olsen Steel “with prejudice”. He did this before the Third Party Compromise and Release was even looked at or approved by a WCAB judge. Thereby destroying the only leverage I had for a fair settlement offer should the C&R not be approved. Then abandoned me by failing to show up with me at the December 8, 1998, pre-trial conference hearing where Judge Dietterle put an Order Suspending Action (OSA) on the C&R.  My attorneys failed me again by refusing to object to the dollar-for-dollar Petition for Credit of $128,910.35 by Argonaut on December 30, 1998. This attorney abandonment caused me to have to pay for my own surgeries.
In my opinion, Argonauts’ best legal counsel turned out to be my own attorneys, Dean Goetz & Richard Sax. Knowing about the open WCAB case. Why didn’t either one help me when the OSA was issued? Attorneys sure do stick together don’t they!?! Back door dealings in my opinion. They both were my attorneys for the Olsen Steel Lawsuit. Dismissing my case WITH PREJUDICE before WCAB judge even saw or approved the C&R leaves a lot of questions unanswered. They helped Argonaut get away with their BAD-FAITH (BULL DUNG & HAGGLE) TACTICS. FULL STOP!!!!

text:
🦔Turn your sound on for this one. This is what it sounds like to live next to an AI data center, 24 hours a day. In Dowagiac, Michigan, residents sued after a facility run by Hyperscale Data ran around the clock at 78 decibels outside their homes. The company offered to buy their houses rather than fix the noise. One family has lived on that street for nearly a century.

My Take
This isn't one town with one bad facility. Microsoft faces a class-action in Wisconsin over data center noise residents can hear a mile and a half from the property line. In Virginia, one-third of data centers sit within 200 feet of homes. Noise from thousands of servers can hit 96 decibels, and diesel backup generators reach 105, which is a jet overhead. Residents report headaches, nausea, and sleep problems. Property values near this kind of infrastructure drop up to 20%. The company response in Michigan was to offer to buy the homes rather than quiet the facility, homes that families spent decades in, priced against a corporate buyout.

Water in Oregon, wells in Georgia, ratepayer costs in Louisiana, river water in California, and now noise in Michigan and Wisconsin. None of this was in the brochure when these projects got approved. Closed-loop cooling and proper sound barriers exist and would solve most of this, but they cost more, so the companies skip them and the neighbors lose sleep and equity instead.

Besides EV West, Grok found the following:

Yes, EV West (San Marcos, California) still offers EV conversion kits for classic cars.54
Their current DIY/build packages (listed as in stock on their site) include purpose-built kits for Volkswagen Beetles/Bugs (e.g., Hyper 9 systems with battery packs for 1956–1977 models), Porsche 911s (Tesla Large Drive Unit packages and AC motor options), Porsche 914s, VW Bus/Type 2, and universal platforms using Tesla drive units or NetGain Hyper 9 motors. They also supply related parts, components, and support, and remain active with products, workshops, and services as of mid-2026.54

Other companies in the US and Canada offering EV conversion kits (or strong kit-oriented options) for classic/vintage cars

Focus is on those providing kits or modular packages suitable for DIY or installer use on classics, rather than purely custom turnkey shop builds only.

United States:
•Flash Drive Motors — Turn-key conversions and DIY EV conversion kits (vehicle-specific and universal). Notable complete bolt-in kits for classics such as Ford Model A (includes motor, batteries, adapters, etc.).47
•Electric GT (Tremec Electric GT) — Plug-and-play / “e-Crate” or eMotor Block systems designed as complete, pre-assembled EV packages for vehicle integration and aftermarket conversions. Includes systems targeted at classic Porsches (e.g., 911/912). Emphasizes ready-to-install rather than pure parts kits.56
•Legacy EV — Complete EV conversion/electrification kits and components (motors, controllers, batteries, wiring, etc.), plus training. Offers modular and more complete packages aimed at conversions.39
•Zelectric Motors (San Diego, CA) — Specializes in converting early Porsches and air-cooled VWs (Beetles, Microbuses, Karmann Ghias, etc.). Primarily known for full conversions/restorations but is a major player in the classic EV space for these platforms.63
Other US shops (e.g., E-Muscle Cars, Foremost EV, Moment Motor Company, Kindred Motorworks) focus more on custom/full-shop classic EV conversions and restomods rather than selling broad DIY kits.

Canada:
•CanEV (Canadian Electric Vehicles) — Offers complete EV conversion kits (including Hyper 9-based systems with battery packs) for vehicles such as VW Beetles, Porsche 911/914, Land Rover Defender, and universal platforms. Also sells parts and powertrain solutions.29
•Ingenext (Quebec) — Supplies Tesla-based conversion components, motor/battery controllers, kits/packages, and support for EV swaps (including classics). They assist with conversions and sell related hardware.69

Availability, pricing, specific vehicle fitment, and stock change, so check the companies’ websites directly for current kits, lead times, and technical details. Many kits range from partial/universal starter packages to more complete vehicle-specific systems (often tens of thousands of dollars depending on batteries and power level). Professional installation or significant fabrication skills are typically required for safety and performance.

Justice demands that Harry and his band of greedy, exploitative chancers and blackmailers are not allowed to hide behind the unwarranted claims of their very presentable and capable  KC Nicholas Bacon, but that they're made to swallow in full the draught of poison they so maliciously prepared for Associated Newspapers to swallow.

I know NIck Bacon and have a great deal of repesct for his abilities, which I personally experienced when  he represented me against some dodgy soilcitors some years ago.

It tickles me to see how my very capable barrister of old has gone from well deserved strength to strength as his career has taken him to the legal heights he so richly deserves to scale.

He has had the thankless task in the last few days of putting forth the reasons why the Claimants such as Prince Harry and the other equally discreditable chancers  in this notorious Associated Newspapers case do not deserve to be stuck with the millions of pounds of costs they deliberately ran up.

Mr Justice Nicklin, a judge I have much respect for, having appeared before him in my libel action against The Daily Mirror, will hopefully take the hard line Anthony White KC for Associated has agrued for.

That sickening cabal of claimants, barristers and solicitors, are hoping to avoid being penalised                                       for their egregious and, in my opinion, shockingly disgraceful actions, many of which were on the wrong side of the law and some deserving of imprisonment as they set about fabricating the most outrageous con on Associated Newspapers.

Nick has taken the pains to make the fallacious pojnt that the Claimants brought the action in good faith, and therefore they do not deserve to be penalised with costs on an indemnity basis.

All the evidence points to the fact that they did not bring the case in good faith, but set about fabricating one that they knew was unmerited and should never have been brought, and would never have been, had the claimants not been greedy but also had more ominious objectives than the mere milking of a rich company out of millions.

Standard costs stick the winning side with a proportion of the costs, while indemnity costs do so.

In other words, Nick has been agruing that since the Claimants were acting in good faith (which they patently were not), and they sincerely believed in the virtue of their cause (let's not forget that even Adolf Hilter believed in the virtues of Nazism), Associated Newspapers should be stuck with the millions the claimants would otherwise have to pay it.

No one can accuse me of having been a friend of Associated Newspapers. I have successfully sued them several times over the last five decades.  I have frequently called them out for behaviour I regarded as questionable.

I even had cause, when Paul Dacre wanted to wrest serialisation of my Queen Mother biography from the Sunday Times, to call into question his modus operandi and to tell his representative that I did not like his behaviour, that it had  convinced me to  prefer The Sunday Times offer,  and indeed I regarded him as so unspeakable that she should tell him I was sending a personal message along the lines that he could go fuque himself as I had no intention of allowing him to screw me.

In response, the Mail on Sunday  ran a spoiler on the same day The Sunday Times ran its serialisation, lifting quotes which the Mail used to reveal that I had quoted the Duke of Windsor asserting that he believed the late Queen Mother was the progeny of the cook Marguerite Rodier and the then Lord Glamis.

I deplored the Mail's conduct then, and to say that I am no fan of  Paul Dacre doesn't negate the fact that he and Associated Newspapers deserve my support and the support of all right-thinking believers in a free press in respect of the disgraceful, unlawful and frankly criminal lawsuit Prince Harry, Elton John, David Furnish, Elizabeth Hurley, Sadie Frost, Sir Simon Hughes, and Lady Lawrence brought against Associated.

Associated Newspapers' conduct throught this case has been an exemplar in courage. They have resisted  the forces of a malign set of conspirators who wanted to extort millions out of the newspaper company, orchestrate a campaign of vilification that would result in its closure, with the objective of also creating a second Levenson Enquiry so that Hugh Grant could thereafter have his cock sucked in California without anyone in Britain knowing about it. Meanwhile Harry and Meghan could play at being victims while bullying people left, right and centre, with Hacked Off and its sick sidesick Byline Times continuing to foment faux complaints against journalists such as Dan Wootton, whom they hoped to have locked up for a good ten or twenty years in either England or Scotland for no other offence than disapproving of the antics of the disgraced Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

What we have been dealing with here is not only a greedy legal ieviathan driven by the talented and rapacious David Sherborne, and his band of money-grubbing followers who have posed as victims when in fact half the time they've been anything but, but we are also witness to the overt misuse of the law to fabricate and concoct meretricious legal complaints which would a) bring a lot of profit to the lawyers as well as to the claimants while shutting down one of the most powerful newspapers in the country as they set about muzzling the press and, through that process, you and me.

Mr Justice Nicklin should give the world the message that English  justice is still just, that when a band of chancers, crooks and shyters set about using the legal system to the detriment of the innocent, IRRESPECTIVE of who they are, how famous, celebrated, or royally connected, the Courts will not play along with their abuses, but will ensure that they are made to pay in full for their vicious, egregious, cavalier, irresponsible, arrogant, over-reaching and contemptuous misconduct.

If ever a case called out for the application of indemnity costs, it is this one.

I say this as someone who has suffered far more damage to my life at the hands of the British press generally and Associated Newspapers in particular, than any one of those Claimaints has suffered. Their behaviour has been a study in the arrogance of the privileged and their expectation that they would somehow always manage to escape the more extreme consequences of their choices.

I call upon Mr Justice Nicklin to show them and the world that NO ONE is above the law. No one should be able to misuse the law the way they heve done. They, and not Associated Newspapers, should suffer the loss of the £18,000,000 Associated will otherwise be made to suffer.

In this instance, standard costs would be piling injustice upon injustice, and I sincerely hope Mr Justice Nicklin will show us what true mettle is as he applies justice with the fairness it requires.

During the Cold War, hundreds of American neighborhoods unknowingly sat beside one of the nation's most closely guarded military secrets.

From 1954 through the mid-1970s, the U.S. Army built nearly 300 Nike missile sites around major cities to defend against Soviet bombers. 

Hidden beneath suburban landscapes, these bases combined radar stations with underground launch facilities housing Nike Ajax and later nuclear-capable Nike Hercules missiles, ready to launch within minutes.

Unlike remote military bases, many Nike sites stood beside neighborhoods, schools, and farms, where everyday life unfolded just beyond the fence line. 

As intercontinental ballistic missiles replaced bomber threats, the Nike system became obsolete, and nearly all sites closed by the mid-1970s.

Many former missile bases have since been transformed into parks, schools, warehouses, and nature preserves, while others remain abandoned and overgrown. 

The restored Nike Missile Site SF-88 in California offers one of the few opportunities to see this hidden chapter of Cold War history brought back to life.

Strategic Value for a Financial Institution

A National, Not Regional, Footprint: While teams like Penn State or Texas dominate their specific states and surrounding regions, Notre Dame's fanbase is famously decentralized. If your financial institution is looking for brand exposure that reaches executives in Chicago, wealth managers in New York, and retail customers in California simultaneously, Notre Dame provides that coast-to-coast reach.

High Net-Worth Alumni Base: Notre Dame's alumni and "subway alumni" (fans who did not attend but fiercely support the school) frequently index high in household income and educational attainment. This is an ideal demographic pipeline for premium credit products, wealth management services, and long-term investment accounts.

Brand Prestige: Aligning a financial brand with Notre Dame signals tradition, stability, and institutional excellence—core tenets that consumers look for when deciding where to place their money.

If your goal is deep regional penetration, a top Big Ten or SEC school might still edge them out. However, if you want a premium, national billboard that speaks directly to a high-earning, fiercely loyal demographic, Notre Dame is arguably in a class of its own.

WATCH ME BUILD AN AI BUSINESS FROM SCRATCH (EPISODE 1)

I'm building an AI services business from scratch, on camera, with 4 rules: 

-100% cold outreach
-No audience
-No network
-60 minutes a day max

The scoreboard is how many days it takes a total stranger to pay me $500. Here's the entire model:

1) The niche is tree services in Charlotte. High ticket, no private equity, and after-hours emergencies where the first person to answer wins the job.

2) The offer: a built and hosted website, an AI-powered speed-to-quote form, and a Google Business Profile cleanup. $500 flat.

3) The website IS the lead magnet. We build it first, give it away free, and charge $500 to install and host it.

4) Five agents inside @hyperagentapp run everything. Prospector, Opener, Sitesmith, Fulfiller, and an Account Manager upsell.

5) The Prospector dispatched 8 subagents, scraped 494 businesses, and verified 98 real leads. Done in 30 minutes.

6) The competition is a joke. The first five "websites" on my list: a blank page, a 404, two dead links, and a redirect to a crypto gaming site.

7) First-touch texts: under 160 characters, no links, no emojis, no mention of AI. "Hey, do y'all still do tree removal in Charlotte? Found you on Google. Corey."

8) The agent wrote "y'all" on its own. Sounding like a neighbor, not a company, is the whole reply-rate game.

9) 60 minutes a day covers 25-50 outreach attempts. Outreach is the only work that actually makes money.

10) All 5 agents get given away free in episode 4, plus $1,000 in free Hyperagent credits at the link in the YouTube subscription. Enough to run my entire lead scrape 6 times over.

Two things that I'm looking to accomplish here:

1) Strip away every advantage and prove the model still works. If it works with no audience and one hour a day, nobody has an excuse left.

text:
Happy birthday to former Sand Springs, University of Tulsa and NFL running back and high school and college football coach JR Boone, born on this day in 1925 in Clinton.

Boone was an All-Twin V Conference and All-State selection at running back as a senior at Sand Springs, helping the 1942 Sandite team go 8-2, scoring 99 of the team's 200 points that season.

He also played baseball and basketball for the Sandites and was awarded the Apollo Cup, which went to Sand Springs' outstanding senior athlete.

He then attended the University of Tulsa, where he lettered in football four seasons, leading the Golden Hurricane in rushing yards (661) and scoring (61) as well as kickoff return yards (270 on 8 returns).

He also played baseball, basketball and ran track and field at TU.

In 1948, Boone was selected by the Chicago Bears in the NFL Draft and was also drafted by the New York Yankees of Major League Baseball.

He opted for a pro football career and as a rookie he finished second on the team with seven touchdowns and 589 all purpose yards.

He played four seasons in Chicago before playing the 1952 season with the San Francisco 49ers, where he was second on the team in receiving yards (461).

He finished his career with the Green Bay Packers in 1953 and retired from pro football in 1954.

Boone was known for his toughness. In 1949, he suffered a broken leg while playing baseball during the summer and not only completed playing in that game, he played a second game the next night and another a few days later before discovering the extent of the injury.

Following his playing career, Boone went into coaching, first as an assistant at Selma High School in California and then as head coach at Lindsay and Sanger high schools, where his teams won or tied for conference championships six times.

In 1966, Boone was hired at Reedley Junior College. In seven seasons as head coach, his teams finished either first or second in the conference and he had an overall record of 53-15-3, including 33-7 in conference games. His 1971 team won the California State Junior College football championship.

His success at Reedley led him to be offered the head coaching position at Fresno State University in 1973, where he spent three seasons, his best coming in 1974 when the Bulldogs went 5-7.

Following the 1975 season, Boone resigned to go into private business.

Boone was inducted into the Fresno County Athletic Hall of Fame in 1972, the University of Tulsa Athletic Hall of Fame in 1999, the Reedley College Hall of Fame in 2000. He is also a member of the California Junioe College Hall of Fame and YMCA Hall of Fame.

Boone passed away in 2012 at the age of 86. He was laid to rest in the Chapel of the Light Columbarium and Cemetery in Fresno.

Happy birthday JR! #tdfn #okpreps @SS_SanditeFB @TulsaFootball @ChicagoBears

text:
How can we optimize teaching during complex surgical cases while ensuring patient safety?

This week on BackTable Uro, Vanderbilt Urology colleagues @RuchikaTalwarMD and Dr. Kelvin Moses discuss workflows and advice for teaching successfully intraoperatively, particularly in cases that may demand greater cognitive load and preparedness. A great listen for those involved in surgical education - and tips are offered for trainees as well!

Listen to this episode here: https://t.co/AqJ5y5QeZz
